rw: An ad hominem argument rejects a claim by attacking the speaker's character or traits instead of the reasoning, which is a fallacy because the person's traits do not decide whether a claim is true.

ww.Attacking the argument with evidence and: Attacking the argument with evidence and facts is legitimate criticism that engages the claim itself, so it is the opposite of an ad hominem, which avoids the claim entirely.
ww.Praising the evidence that was presented: Praising the evidence is simply agreement with the case being made, and it does not attack anyone, so it cannot be an ad hominem argument, which is a personal attack.
ww.Asking a question about the whole argume: Asking a question about the whole argument is a fair way to examine its logic, not an attack on the speaker, so it does not match the ad hominem fallacy.

rw: The speaker rejects the proposal by pointing to the author's newness rather than any flaw in the numbers, which is the classic pattern of an ad hominem fallacy that attacks the person.

ww.A sound argument here: Dismissing a budget only because its author is new offers no reasoning about the budget itself, so it cannot be called a sound argument, since sound arguments rely on relevant premises.
ww.A fact from the data: Being new at work is not a fact drawn from data about the budget proposal, so this statement cannot be a fact from the data; it is just a personal remark.
ww.A sound deduction: A sound deduction needs true premises that logically force a conclusion, and being new does not logically imply an untrustworthy budget, so this reasoning is not a valid deduction at all.

rw: A cost-benefit analysis weighs the expected costs of a choice against its expected benefits, so a decision maker can see whether the gains outweigh the expenses before committing money.

ww.Measuring customer complaints each month: Measuring customer complaints each month is a quality or service tracking activity, and it does not compare the costs of a choice with its benefits, so it is not this analysis.
ww.Listing all company assets and debts: Listing all assets and debts describes a balance sheet, which shows what a firm owns and owes at one time, and not a comparison of a proposal's costs with its benefits.
ww.Counting all the employees in a firm: Counting all the employees is a headcount exercise used for staffing records, and it says nothing about weighing costs against benefits for a decision, so it is not a cost-benefit analysis.

rw: Net benefit equals benefit minus cost, so $45,000 minus $30,000 leaves $15,000, which is the real gain the company keeps after paying for the project.

ww.$30,000: The $30,000 figure is only the project's cost, and net benefit means the savings minus the cost, so using the cost alone ignores the $45,000 of expected savings entirely.
ww.$45,000: The $45,000 figure is the gross saving, but net benefit subtracts the $30,000 spent to get it, so $45,000 overstates the gain by the full cost of the project.
ww.$75,000: Adding $30,000 and $45,000 gives $75,000, but a net benefit is found by subtracting cost from benefit, not adding them, so this figure wrongly combines the two amounts.

rw: A pro-and-con list writes the advantages and disadvantages of one option side by side, which helps a person judge the choice before deciding, and that is what the name says.

ww.A list of employees' names for payroll: A list of employees' names for payroll is a staff record used to pay wages, and it does not set out the advantages and disadvantages of any option being considered.
ww.A list of products for sale now: A list of products for sale is a catalog or inventory record, and it does not weigh any option's good and bad points, so it cannot be a pro-and-con list.
ww.A list of expenses for the year: A list of expenses for the year is a budget or accounting record of money spent, and it does not compare the strengths and weaknesses of a choice, so it is not this tool.

rw: A decision matrix lists options in rows and criteria in columns and scores each option on each criterion, so the totals show which choice best fits what matters most.

ww.A table of employee salaries paid: A table of employee salaries is a payroll record that shows what each person is paid, and it does not score competing options against decision criteria, so it is not a decision matrix.
ww.A table of meeting times and rooms: A table of meeting times and rooms is a scheduling tool for booking spaces, and it contains no scoring of options against criteria, so it cannot be a decision matrix.
ww.A table of customer addresses and names: A table of customer addresses and names is a contact database used for mailing, and it does not rate choices on any criteria, so it does not match a decision matrix.

rw: Creative thinking means generating new ideas that are also useful, such as a better product or process, so it combines originality with value rather than novelty alone.

ww.Avoiding all kinds of change: Avoiding all kinds of change is the opposite of creative thinking, which looks for new approaches, and refusing every change would block the fresh ideas that creativity depends on.
ww.Repeating the old methods: Repeating the old methods keeps doing things the familiar way, which is routine thinking, and it produces no new ideas, so it cannot describe creative thinking at all.
ww.Copying other ideas exactly: Copying other ideas exactly adds nothing original, because creative thinking requires producing something new or improved, and a perfect copy is imitation and not creation.

rw: Data-driven decision making means gathering relevant facts, analyzing them, and letting the results guide the choice, which reduces guesswork and makes decisions easier to justify and to review later.

ww.Ignoring all numbers and facts on hand: Ignoring numbers and facts is the reverse of data-driven decision making, which depends on evidence, so a choice made while ignoring the data is a guess and not data driven.
ww.Letting the loudest voice in the room de: Letting the loudest voice decide bases the choice on personality and not evidence, so it is the opposite of a data-driven approach, which weighs facts over who speaks most forcefully.
ww.Choosing by gut feeling with no data: Choosing by gut feeling with no data relies on intuition alone, which is the contrast of a data-driven method, since that method requires evidence to support each decision made.

rw: Before blaming the price, she should check other causes such as competitors' actions, seasonal demand and advertising changes, because sales may have fallen for reasons unrelated to the 15% price rise.

ww.Assume the price rise is the only cause: Assuming the price rise is the only cause ignores other possible factors and commits the fallacy of assuming one event caused another just because it happened first.
ww.Fire the sales team at once to cut costs: Firing the sales team at once is a drastic action with no evidence linking staff to the 15% drop, and it would not reveal what truly caused the decline.
ww.Ignore the data and carry on as before: Ignoring the data and carrying on leaves a 15% sales fall unexamined, so the real cause stays unknown and a fixable problem could keep hurting the firm's revenue.

rw: Correlation means two variables move together, while causation means one actually produces a change in the other, and the first does not prove the second without further evidence.

ww.Correlation always proves a cause of the: Saying correlation always proves a cause is false, because two things can move together by chance or through a third factor, such as ice cream sales and sunburn both rising in summer.
ww.They are exactly the same thing in every: The two ideas are not the same, because many pairs of things rise and fall together with no cause between them, so treating them as identical leads to false conclusions.
ww.Causation means they never move together: Causation does not mean the two never move together; a real cause usually does show up as a pattern, so saying they never move together has the relationship backward.

rw: Customer service is the help and support a business gives customers before, during and after a sale, such as advice, order handling and problem solving, which builds satisfaction and repeat business.

ww.The delivery truck's route to the stores: The delivery truck's route is a logistics matter about moving goods, and it describes distribution and not the help and support offered to customers around a purchase.
ww.The advertising of a product on the radi: Advertising on the radio is a form of promotion meant to attract buyers, and it is not the assistance given to customers before, during and after a sale.
ww.The price of a product in the store wind: The price shown in a store window is a pricing decision, which tells shoppers the cost of an item, and it does not describe the help given to customers.

rw: Customer loyalty is a customer's habit of choosing the same business again and again, built through good service and quality, which gives a firm steady sales and often free recommendations.

ww.A customer who avoids the store: A customer who avoids the store shows the lack of loyalty, since loyal customers keep returning, and staying away is the opposite behavior from the repeat buying that loyalty means.
ww.A customer who buys only one time: A customer who buys only one time has not shown a repeat pattern, and loyalty needs repeated purchases over time, so a single purchase does not demonstrate loyalty to the business.
ww.A customer who always asks for refunds: Always asking for refunds shows dissatisfaction with what was bought, which is not loyalty, since a loyal customer is satisfied enough to keep buying and not return goods.

rw: CRM refers to tools and systems that record, manage and analyze a company's contact with customers, helping it understand needs, track sales and improve service and long term relationships.

ww.A system for managing staff schedules an: Managing staff schedules and shifts is a workforce scheduling function, and it focuses on employees and not on tracking and analyzing a firm's contacts with its customers.
ww.A system for managing company taxes and: Managing company taxes and filings is an accounting and compliance task that concerns government paperwork, and it has no link to storing and studying customer contact and history.
ww.A system for managing a warehouse and it: Managing a warehouse and its stock describes inventory management software, which tracks goods held for sale, and not a system built to manage and analyze customer relationships.

rw: The best first response is to listen to the customer, apologize sincerely and offer a solution, because this shows respect, calms the situation and starts fixing the problem that upset them.

ww.Tell the customer to complain elsewhere: Telling the customer to complain elsewhere dismisses their concern and will probably lose their business, since an unresolved complaint pushes a person toward competitors and bad reviews.
ww.Argue that the delay was not the company: Arguing that the delay was not the company's fault puts the firm on the defensive and ignores the customer's frustration, which usually makes the situation worse and damages trust.
ww.Ignore the complaint and hope it fades a: Ignoring the complaint and hoping it fades leaves the customer without any answer, and an unhandled complaint often grows into lost sales and negative word of mouth.

rw: A supplier is a business that sells goods or materials to another business, such as a flour mill selling to a bakery, which makes it a source of inputs for the buyer.

ww.A customer who buys goods from the firm: A customer buys goods from the firm, while a supplier sells goods to it, so describing a customer as a supplier reverses the direction in which goods and money flow.
ww.A rival in the same market selling goods: A rival selling in the same market is a competitor, which competes for the same customers, and does not provide goods or materials to the firm, so it is not a supplier.
ww.A regulator who inspects goods and sites: A regulator who inspects goods and sites enforces rules and standards, which is an oversight role, and it does not sell goods to a business, so it is not a supplier.

rw: Strong supplier relationships help secure dependable quality, fair pricing and on-time delivery, which keep production running smoothly and protect the firm from shortages, delays and sudden cost increases.

ww.To avoid paying invoices on time or at a: Avoiding payment of invoices would harm trust and probably end the supply, and it is not a reason for building strong relationships, which rest on honest and fair dealing.
ww.To make suppliers dependent on the busin: Making suppliers dependent on the business is not the goal; good relationships are built on mutual benefit, and a dependent supplier may leave or resent the one-sided arrangement.
ww.To keep suppliers from talking to compet: Keeping suppliers from talking to competitors is not a realistic or ethical aim, and strong relationships are about cooperation and reliability and not about controlling who a supplier speaks to.

rw: Networking means building and keeping professional contacts, such as colleagues and industry peers, who can share advice, job leads and opportunities that help a career and a business grow.

ww.Selling to strangers door to door: Selling to strangers door to door is direct selling, which pushes products to buyers, and it does not describe building a network of professional contacts for mutual benefit.
ww.Connecting computers in an office: Connecting computers in an office is computer networking, a technical meaning of the word, but in business relationships networking refers to people and not to machines or cables.
ww.Working alone on every task: Working alone on every task is the reverse of networking, which depends on meeting and connecting with other people, so isolation cannot be the meaning of the term.

rw: Professional etiquette is the set of polite and respectful rules for behaving at work, such as courtesy, punctuality and good manners, which helps people cooperate and builds a good reputation.

ww.A list of the firm's products: A list of the firm's products is a catalog and has nothing to do with how employees behave, so it cannot define professional etiquette in the workplace.
ww.A set of tax rules for companies: A set of tax rules for companies is a legal and accounting subject about money owed to government, and it says nothing about courtesy or conduct between coworkers.
ww.A dress code for parties and clubs: A dress code for parties and clubs concerns social settings, while professional etiquette covers conduct in the workplace, including manners, communication and respect, so this answer is too narrow and misplaced.

rw: Talking calmly and seeking solutions addresses the problem directly and respectfully, which lets both people explain their views and find a fix that keeps the working relationship intact.

ww.Gossip about them to others: Gossiping about a coworker spreads rumors, harms trust and does nothing to settle the disagreement, so it makes the conflict worse and damages your own professional reputation.
ww.Avoid them for as long as you can: Avoiding the coworker for as long as you can leaves the problem unresolved, and unspoken tension usually grows, so avoidance delays a solution and hurts teamwork.
ww.Raise your voice before others: Raising your voice in front of others humiliates the coworker, escalates the conflict and looks unprofessional, so it is more likely to create anger than to settle the issue.

rw: Negotiation is a discussion between two or more parties aimed at reaching an agreement they can both accept, usually through offers, concessions and compromise on the points in dispute.

ww.A lawsuit filed in court: A lawsuit filed in court is a formal legal action to settle a dispute by a judge, and it is not the give-and-take discussion that negotiation describes.
ww.A refusal to talk with anyone: A refusal to talk with anyone is the opposite of negotiation, which requires both sides to communicate, so ending all conversation makes an agreement impossible.
ww.A one-sided demand with no give: A one-sided demand with no give is an ultimatum and not a negotiation, because negotiation involves both parties offering concessions and moving toward a result they both can accept.

rw: A service level agreement is a contract that sets out the level of service a provider owes a customer, such as response times and uptime, with consequences if the standards are missed.

ww.A contract for a bank loan to the firm: A contract for a bank loan to the firm is a loan agreement about borrowing money and repayment terms, and it does not set the quality of a service provided.
ww.A contract for buying a building from a: A contract for buying a building from a seller is a real estate purchase agreement, which transfers property, and it does not define a measurable level of service owed.
ww.A contract for hiring a new manager now: A contract for hiring a new manager is an employment agreement, which covers pay and duties of one person, and it does not set service standards between a provider and a client.

rw: A strategic alliance is a cooperative arrangement in which two businesses work together on a shared goal or project while staying separate companies, which fits the description of cooperating on a project.

ww.A hostile takeover bid: A hostile takeover bid is an unwelcome attempt to buy a company against its management's wishes, which is the opposite of cooperating, so it cannot be a partnership.
ww.A monopoly market: A monopoly market has a single seller controlling supply, which is a market structure and not a cooperative arrangement between businesses working together on a project.
ww.A bankruptcy filing: A bankruptcy filing is a legal step taken by a firm that cannot pay its debts, and it does not describe businesses cooperating toward a shared goal.

rw: A vendor code of conduct sets out ethical standards that suppliers must follow, such as fair labor, safety and honest dealing, so the buying company can protect its reputation and values.

ww.A price list for the suppliers: A price list for suppliers is a document of costs and does not state how suppliers must behave, so it does not describe a vendor code of conduct.
ww.A tax form that vendors must file: A tax form that vendors must file is a government reporting document about income, and it does not describe the ethical behavior a company expects from its suppliers.
ww.A shipping label printed for each box: A shipping label printed for each box identifies where a parcel goes, and it is a logistics item that sets no standard for how suppliers should behave.

rw: Public relations is the practice of managing a business's communication with the public and shaping its image, using tools such as press releases, events and responses to news coverage.

ww.Setting product prices for the coming ye: Setting product prices for the coming year is a pricing and marketing decision, and it is not about managing a firm's communication with the public or its image.
ww.Selling products door to door in a neigh: Selling products door to door is direct selling, which aims at making sales, while public relations focuses on reputation and communication and not on personal selling to households.
ww.Managing employees' schedules and work s: Managing employees' schedules and work shifts is a human resources and operations task, and it has no connection to communicating with the public or protecting a company's image.

rw: A quick, honest response with a plan to fix the problem usually preserves part of the customers' trust, though not all of it, because the harm still happened and left a mark.

ww.Customers cheer immediately: Customers are unlikely to cheer immediately after being harmed, since a quick and honest response limits damage but does not erase the harm, so this outcome is too optimistic.
ww.Nothing is affected at all: Saying nothing is affected at all ignores that the product caused harm, which will naturally affect how customers see the firm, even when it responds well afterward.
ww.Trust is completely lost: Trust being completely lost is too extreme when the company responds quickly, honestly and with a repair plan, because those actions usually help customers forgive and keep some confidence.

rw: A stakeholder analysis identifies the groups affected by a project or decision, such as employees, customers and owners, and weighs their interests and influence so managers can plan how to engage them.

ww.Counting a company's shares each quarter: Counting a company's shares each quarter-end is a record of ownership and has nothing to do with finding the groups affected by a decision and what they want.
ww.Reviewing a financial statement for prof: Reviewing a financial statement for profit is an accounting exercise about money results, and it does not identify the people or groups whose interests a decision affects.
ww.Testing a product before it is sold to b: Testing a product before it is sold to buyers is quality or market testing, and it does not map the groups affected by a project and their interests.

rw: Stress is the body's reaction to demands or pressure, which may trigger faster heartbeat, tension and worry, and can help in short bursts but harm health if it lasts.

ww.A feeling of total relaxation after a br: A feeling of total relaxation after a break is the opposite of stress, which involves tension, so relaxation cannot be the definition of the body's response to pressure.
ww.A work schedule for staff members at a f: A work schedule for staff is a planning document that lists shifts, and it is not a physical or mental reaction, so it cannot define stress.
ww.A type of exercise done in a gym each da: A type of exercise done in a gym is physical activity, which may help reduce stress, but it is not itself the body's reaction to pressure that stress means.

rw: Tight deadlines create time pressure and a feeling of being rushed, which makes them a very common source of workplace stress for many employees.

ww.Fair workloads: Fair workloads are a healthy condition that reduces pressure on employees, so they work against stress and cannot be called a common workplace stressor.
ww.Helpful coworkers: Helpful coworkers give support and share tasks, which reduces strain, so they act as a stress buffer and not as a workplace stressor.
ww.Clear expectations: Clear expectations tell workers what to do, which lowers uncertainty and anxiety, so they reduce stress and are not a stressor; unclear expectations would be the stressor instead.

rw: Exercise, sleep and a talk with a trusted person all reduce tension and restore energy, which makes this combination a healthy and practical way to manage stress.

ww.Avoiding all problems and work: Avoiding all problems and work does not solve anything, because the pressures remain and tend to pile up, so avoidance raises stress over time instead of reducing it.
ww.Blaming your coworkers for stress: Blaming your coworkers for stress damages relationships and does not remove the cause of the pressure, so it adds conflict and offers no healthy way to cope.
ww.Skipping sleep to work more each night: Skipping sleep to work more tires the body and mind, lowering focus and health, which increases stress and mistakes, so it is a harmful way to cope.

rw: Time management means planning how you spend your time on goals and tasks, using tools like schedules and priorities, so important work gets done without last minute pressure.

ww.Doing tasks in random order each day: Doing tasks in random order each day wastes time and misses priorities, which is poor organization and not time management, which involves deliberate planning of how to use time.
ww.Delaying all work until the deadline: Delaying all work until the deadline is procrastination, which causes stress and rushed work, and it is the opposite of managing time wisely across a project.
ww.Working without breaks for long hours: Working without breaks for long hours leads to fatigue and weaker output, so it is not good time management, which includes sensible planning and rest to stay productive.

rw: The task that is both urgent and important needs immediate action, because it has a pressing deadline and a significant effect, so it comes before all others in priority.

ww.The urgent but unimportant task: The urgent but unimportant task should be delegated or limited, because it demands attention yet adds little value, so doing it first would waste effort that should go to bigger priorities.
ww.The important but not urgent task: The important but not urgent task should be scheduled for later, since it has no immediate deadline, so it ranks behind a task that is both urgent and important.
ww.The tasks of no urgency or value: Tasks with neither urgency nor value should be dropped or left for last, because they add no benefit and no deadline pressure, so they should never be done first.

rw: The Eisenhower matrix sorts tasks into four boxes by urgency and importance, helping a person decide what to do now, schedule, delegate or drop, which makes it a prioritizing tool.

ww.Calculating payroll for all the staff: Calculating payroll is an accounting task about paying wages, and it does not rank tasks by their urgency and importance, which is what the Eisenhower matrix does.
ww.Tracking inventory in the warehouse: Tracking inventory in the warehouse is a stock control task, and the Eisenhower matrix is not designed for counting goods but for setting priorities among tasks.
ww.Scheduling vacations for the whole staff: Scheduling vacations for the whole staff is a leave planning job, and the Eisenhower matrix does not do this, since it prioritizes tasks instead of arranging time off.

rw: Procrastination means putting off tasks that need to be done, often until the last moment, which creates stress and lowers the quality of the work finally produced.

ww.Planning tasks and doing them early: Planning tasks and doing them early is good time management, and it is the opposite of procrastination, which is the habit of postponing work.
ww.Delegating tasks to other people: Delegating tasks to other people is a leadership technique for sharing work, not delay, so it differs from procrastination, where the person simply fails to start the work.
ww.Completing tasks early each week: Completing tasks early each week is the reverse of procrastination, since it shows prompt action, whereas procrastination is the habit of postponing work until it becomes urgent.

rw: Burnout is a state of chronic exhaustion, cynicism and reduced performance caused by prolonged work stress, which matches the fatigue and decline this employee shows after months of heavy overtime.

ww.Promotion: A promotion is a step up in position and would not cause constant fatigue and cynicism, so it does not match symptoms of exhaustion after months of overtime.
ww.Motivation: Motivation is a drive to work toward goals, and the employee shows falling interest and performance, which indicates the opposite, so motivation does not fit these symptoms.
ww.Engagement: Engagement means enthusiasm and commitment to work, while this employee is tired, cynical and performing worse, which signals the opposite condition, so engagement is not the right answer.

rw: Setting realistic workloads and giving support reduces pressure and helps employees cope, because they feel capable and backed by their manager, which lowers stress and burnout risk.

ww.Ignore employee concerns completely: Ignoring employee concerns completely leaves problems unsolved and makes people feel unheard, which increases stress and does nothing to help staff cope with pressure.
ww.Set impossible deadlines for the staff: Setting impossible deadlines places unreasonable pressure on staff, which raises stress, so it is a cause of employee stress and not a way to reduce it.
ww.Raise workloads without notice or pay: Raising workloads without notice or pay creates unfairness and overload, which increases stress and resentment, so it harms employees and does not help reduce their stress.

rw: Conflict management means handling disagreements constructively and finding solutions the parties can accept, which keeps working relationships healthy and prevents small disputes from growing into larger problems.

ww.Punishing everyone involved in the dispu: Punishing everyone involved in the dispute is unfair and ignores who is at fault, which increases resentment and does not solve the disagreement, so it is not conflict management.
ww.Avoiding all disagreements by staying si: Avoiding all disagreements by staying silent leaves problems unresolved and tension building, whereas conflict management means dealing with disputes openly and constructively.
ww.Winning every argument at any cost to ot: Winning every argument at any cost to others damages relationships and creates new conflict, so it is not conflict management, which seeks outcomes that work for the people involved.

rw: Staying calm, listening and looking for a solution lowers the tension, shows respect and addresses the customer's real problem, which is the best way to handle an angry customer.

ww.Walk away without saying a word to them: Walking away without a word leaves the customer's problem unresolved and appears dismissive, which will probably raise their anger and damage the business's reputation.
ww.Shout back to show who has authority: Shouting back escalates the situation and is unprofessional, since showing authority does nothing to solve the problem and makes an angry customer even angrier.
ww.Blame the customer for the problem: Blaming the customer for the problem puts them on the defensive and ignores their concern, so it worsens the conflict and may lose the customer for good.

rw: Assertive communication means stating your needs and views clearly and respectfully, while still considering other people, which balances honesty with courtesy and helps resolve problems.

ww.Hinting without ever saying what you rea: Hinting without saying what you want is passive communication, because others must guess your needs, so it is not assertive, which requires stating needs clearly.
ww.Staying silent to avoid any kind of conf: Staying silent to avoid conflict is passive behavior that leaves your needs unmet, so it is the opposite of assertive communication, which speaks up honestly and respectfully.
ww.Demanding things aggressively from other: Demanding things aggressively from others is aggressive communication, since it ignores their rights and feelings, and assertive communication differs because it stays respectful.

rw: Resilience is the ability to recover from setbacks, adapt to difficulty and keep going, which helps people and teams handle stress, failure and change without giving up.

ww.Blaming others for failures at work: Blaming others for failures is a way to dodge responsibility and does not help a person recover, so it is not resilience, which means bouncing back.
ww.Giving up when things get hard at work: Giving up when things get hard is the reverse of resilience, which means continuing and recovering after difficulty, so quitting shows a lack of that quality.
ww.Never facing a problem or a setback: Never facing a problem or setback is avoidance, not resilience, since resilience is shown by recovering after real difficulties, which cannot happen if the problems are never faced.

rw: Reviewing what went wrong and adjusting the plan shows resilience, because the team learns from the setback, recovers and continues toward the goal with a better approach.

ww.Quitting the project right away and for: Quitting the project right away and for good is giving up, which is the opposite of resilience, since resilient teams recover from failure and keep working toward the goal.
ww.Hiding the miss from the manager and cli: Hiding the missed deadline from the manager and clients is dishonest and prevents solving the problem, so it is not resilience, which depends on facing setbacks openly.
ww.Blaming one person and moving on with no: Blaming one person and moving on with no changes avoids learning from the failure, so the same problem will probably recur, which means it does not show resilience.

rw: A deadline is a specific time by which a task must be completed, which gives people a clear target and helps teams plan their work and prioritize.

ww.A tool for tracking costs and spending: A tool for tracking costs and spending describes a budget or accounting method, and it does not set the time by which a task must be finished.
ww.A suggestion for finishing whenever poss: A suggestion for finishing whenever possible lacks a firm date, while a deadline is a fixed limit, so a loose suggestion does not define a deadline.
ww.A reward for finishing a task early: A reward for finishing a task early is an incentive, which is a different idea from a deadline, which is the time limit and not a prize.

rw: Smaller tasks make a large project feel manageable and easier to track, because progress can be seen step by step, which reduces overwhelm and helps teams meet deadlines.

ww.It makes the whole project much longer: Breaking a project into smaller tasks does not make the whole project longer; it organizes the same work into steps, so claiming it lengthens the project is incorrect.
ww.It removes the need for planning of any: Breaking a project into tasks actually requires careful planning, so it does not remove the need for planning; it is part of how planning is done.
ww.It increases confusion for the team: Dividing a project into smaller tasks usually clarifies who does what, so it reduces confusion and does not increase it for the team, which is the opposite effect.

rw: Asking for help when overwhelmed gets support that can reduce the workload and prevent mistakes, which protects both the person's wellbeing and the quality and timeliness of the work.

ww.It is never allowed at work by any manag: Asking for help is allowed and often encouraged by managers, so claiming it is never allowed at work by any manager is false and discourages people from seeking support.
ww.It always makes tasks harder to finish o: Asking for help does not always make tasks harder to finish on time; it often speeds work by sharing the load, so the word always makes this statement wrong.
ww.Asking for help is a sign of failure, so: Asking for help is not a sign of failure but a sensible step, and going alone when overwhelmed raises the risk of errors and burnout, so this advice is harmful.

rw: Transactional leadership relies on exchanges, rewarding employees who meet targets and correcting those who fall short, which matches a manager who rewards quotas and corrects those who miss them.

ww.Transformational leadership: Transformational leadership inspires people with a vision and personal growth, not mainly rewards and corrections tied to quotas, so it does not match a reward-and-correct approach.
ww.Servant-style leadership: Servant-style leadership puts the needs of followers first and focuses on supporting them, which differs from rewarding quota success and correcting failures, so it does not fit.
ww.Laissez-faire leadership: Laissez-faire leadership gives employees freedom with little direction, so a manager who actively rewards and corrects performance is not using that hands-off style.

rw: Democratic leadership involves team members in decisions by seeking their input and ideas, which builds commitment and uses the group's knowledge, though decisions can take longer to reach.

ww.Making all decisions alone each day: Making all decisions alone each day describes autocratic leadership, where one person holds control, which is the opposite of democratic leadership that shares decisions with the team.
ww.Letting no one decide anything at all: Letting no one decide anything leads to confusion and drift, and it is not democratic leadership, which depends on active participation and an actual decision at the end.
ww.Voting on trivial items only in a year: Voting only on trivial items once a year gives staff almost no real voice, so it is token consultation and not the genuine involvement that democratic leadership requires.

rw: Autocratic leadership lets one person decide quickly without debate, which suits an emergency where there is no time to consult others and instant action is needed.

ww.Delay until all agree: Delaying until all agree wastes time that an emergency does not allow, so waiting for consensus can make the crisis worse and it is not suitable here.
ww.Laissez-faire leadership: Laissez-faire leadership leaves decisions to the team with little direction, which could cause confusion and delay when instant, coordinated action is required during an emergency.
ww.Group votes on every step: Group votes on every step take too much time during an emergency, so a democratic process of voting is too slow when instant action is needed.

rw: A delegating leader should provide clear expectations, the necessary resources and the authority to finish the task, so the employee knows the goal and can act without constant approval.

ww.No guidance at all and no resources to f: Giving no guidance and no resources sets the employee up to fail, because delegation requires the means to complete the task, so this leaves the person unable to succeed.
ww.Constant monitoring of every step so the: Constant monitoring of every step is micromanagement, which defeats the purpose of delegation by removing the employee's independence and wasting the leader's time, so it is not the right support.
ww.A vague deadline and no clear instructio: A vague deadline and unclear instructions leave the employee guessing what is wanted and when, which makes success unlikely, so this is poor delegation and not good support.

rw: In the forming stage the group first meets, members are polite and unsure, and roles and goals are unclear, so people look to the leader for direction.

ww.The group ends the project for good now: The group ending the project for good describes the adjourning stage, which comes last, so it is not the forming stage, which comes at the beginning.
ww.The group argues about roles and tasks: Arguing about roles and tasks is the storming stage, where conflict appears, and it comes after forming, so it does not describe the first stage.
ww.The group works at peak from the start: Working at peak from the start is the performing stage, which comes only after the group has formed, argued and settled its norms, so it cannot describe forming.

rw: In the storming stage, conflict arises as members disagree over roles, tasks and approaches, and the group must work through these tensions before it can move on to norming.

ww.Members set shared norms and team goals: Setting shared norms and team goals is the norming stage, which follows storming, so this describes a later phase of team development and not the stage of conflict.
ww.Members meet for the first time and are: Meeting for the first time and being polite describes the forming stage, which comes first, so it does not match storming, in which disagreements appear.
ww.Members work smoothly together as a team: Members working smoothly together as a team is the performing stage, which comes after storming, so smooth cooperation does not describe the conflict-filled stage.

rw: In the norming stage the team has settled its rules, roles and expectations and begins to cooperate and build trust, which matches this team that has settled its rules.

ww.Forming: Forming is the first stage, when members meet and are unsure of roles, so it does not match a team that has already settled its rules and is cooperating.
ww.Storming: Storming is the stage of conflict over roles and approaches, and this team has already settled its rules and cooperates, which means it has moved beyond that stage.
ww.Adjourning: Adjourning is the final stage, when the team wraps up and disbands, and this team is still working together, so it has not reached that point.

rw: Encouraging a devil's advocate invites someone to challenge ideas and raise objections, which exposes weak assumptions and prevents the group from agreeing too quickly, so it reduces groupthink.

ww.Punish anyone who disagrees with the lea: Punishing anyone who disagrees with the leader silences dissent, which strengthens groupthink since members will stay quiet and agree, and so it makes the problem worse.
ww.Decide before any discussion to save the: Deciding before any discussion removes the chance to hear different views, so it increases groupthink by treating one idea as settled and ignoring useful alternatives.
ww.Only listen to the leader and no one els: Listening only to the leader shuts out other views and encourages conformity, which feeds groupthink, since good decisions need a range of opinions from many group members.

rw: Social loafing is the tendency of people to put in less effort when working in a group than they would alone, often because individual contributions are hard to see.

ww.Working extra hard in a group when watch: Working extra hard when watched is a different effect, sometimes called social facilitation, while social loafing is the opposite, a drop in effort that happens in groups.
ww.Leaving the team for another firm in tow: Leaving the team for another firm is employee turnover, which concerns quitting, and it is not the reduced effort of members who stay in a group.
ww.Socializing after work with the whole te: Socializing after work with the team is a social activity and not a reduction in effort during group tasks, so it does not describe social loafing.

rw: Assigning clear individual roles and accountability makes each person's contribution visible and expected, so members cannot hide behind the group, which reduces social loafing.

ww.Make tasks vague so no one knows who doe: Making tasks vague so no one knows who does what hides individual contributions, which encourages social loafing, so it makes the problem worse and does not reduce it.
ww.Remove all deadlines so tasks can drift: Removing all deadlines lets work drift and lowers pressure to contribute, which tends to increase social loafing and does not help reduce it in a group.
ww.Reward only the loudest voice in the gro: Rewarding only the loudest voice ignores quiet contributors and encourages talking over doing, which hurts fairness and motivation, so it does not reduce social loafing.

rw: Restating what you heard and checking whether it is right shows you are paying attention and confirms understanding, which are the key features of active listening.

ww.'Can we skip this and move on to the nex: Asking to skip the topic and move on shows no interest in the coworker's problem, so it ignores the speaker and is not active listening.
ww.'Let me tell you my story instead, as I: Taking over with your own story shifts the focus from the speaker to yourself, so it does not show you understood the problem and is not active listening.
ww.'I already know all that, so go on to th: Saying you already know it all and asking to move on dismisses the coworker and shows no effort to understand, so it is the opposite of active listening.

rw: A feedback loop is a process where receivers respond to the sender, so the sender can confirm the message was understood and adjust it if needed, making communication two-way.

ww.A written policy manual that staff read: A written policy manual that staff read once is a one-time document with no exchange of responses, so it does not describe a feedback loop, which is a continuing exchange.
ww.A one-way announcement with no reply, fr: A one-way announcement with no reply lacks any response from the receivers, so it is the opposite of a feedback loop, which depends on communication returning to the sender.
ww.A schedule of meetings kept by the manag: A schedule of meetings kept by managers is a planning calendar and not a communication process in which receivers respond, so it is not a feedback loop.

rw: Asking staff to reply with their understanding builds feedback into the message, so the manager can confirm that the instructions were understood and correct any misunderstanding early.

ww.Avoiding communication with all the staf: The manager is communicating with staff and asking for a reply, so this cannot be avoiding communication; it is an active attempt to make the message clear.
ww.Using only nonverbal cues such as a nod: An email asking for written replies uses written words and not just nonverbal cues like a nod, so this is not an example of relying only on nonverbal cues.
ww.Removing all feedback from the whole sta: The manager is asking for replies, which adds feedback, so this is the opposite of removing all feedback; it brings feedback into the process to check understanding.

rw: A communication barrier is anything that blocks a message from being understood, such as noise, jargon, language differences or distraction, which stops the receiver from getting the intended meaning.

ww.A friendly greeting that opens a message: A friendly greeting that opens a message helps communication and does not block understanding, so it is not a barrier; it is a courtesy that supports the message.
ww.A shared language between the sender and: A shared language helps a sender and receiver understand each other, so it removes a barrier and does not create one; a language difference would be the barrier.
ww.A clear, simple message the listener gra: A clear, simple message the listener grasps at once supports communication, so it is the opposite of a barrier, which makes understanding harder.

rw: Technical jargon that the audience does not know confuses listeners and blocks understanding, so it is a barrier when speaking to a general audience who lack that specialized vocabulary.

ww.Giving examples to the listeners present: Giving examples helps the audience connect with ideas and understand them, so it supports communication and does not act as a barrier for a general audience.
ww.Checking for questions at the talk's end: Checking for questions at the end of a talk invites feedback and clears up confusion, so it helps understanding and is not a communication barrier.
ww.Using plain language that they all know: Plain language that everyone knows makes the message easy to follow, so it removes barriers and does not create one for a general audience.

rw: A win-win negotiation ends with an outcome where both sides benefit, usually because they focus on shared interests, which keeps the relationship healthy and makes agreements more likely to last.

ww.No agreement is reached by either side: No agreement being reached by either side is a failed negotiation, sometimes called no deal, and it does not give both parties a benefit, so it is not win-win.
ww.Both sides lose something of value: Both sides losing something of value is a lose-lose outcome, which is worse than win-win, where each party leaves with a real gain, so this is incorrect.
ww.One side wins everything it asked for: One side winning everything it asked for is a win-lose outcome, since the other party gets nothing, so it does not describe a win-win negotiation.

rw: Mediation uses a neutral third party who helps the disputants talk and reach their own agreement, without imposing a decision, which keeps the solution voluntary and acceptable to both.

ww.A judge ordering a result after a full c: A judge ordering a result after a full court hearing is litigation, in which an authority decides, whereas mediation leaves the decision to the disputing parties themselves.
ww.One side deciding for both of the partie: One side deciding for both parties after hearing them is a one-sided ruling, not mediation, because a mediator is neutral and does not decide the outcome for others.
ww.Ignoring the dispute until it fades away: Ignoring the dispute until it fades is avoidance, which leaves the issue unresolved, and it involves no third party helping the parties, so it is not mediation.

rw: Collaborating means working with the other party to find a solution that fully meets both sides' needs, which takes cooperation and open discussion and produces a win-win result.

ww.Competing: Competing is a style where one pursues its own goals at the other's expense, so it does not seek a solution meeting both parties' needs as collaboration does.
ww.Avoidance: Avoidance means sidestepping the conflict and not dealing with it, so neither side's needs are addressed, which is different from working together to meet both needs.
ww.Accommodating: Accommodating means giving in to the other party and putting their needs ahead of your own, so only one side's needs are met, and it is not collaboration.

rw: Compromise happens when each side gives up something to reach an agreement, meeting partway, so both gain part of what they wanted and the dispute ends.

ww.A third party decides for both sides alo: A third party deciding for both sides is arbitration or a ruling, not compromise, in which the two sides themselves bargain and agree on a middle ground.
ww.One side gets everything and the other g: One side getting everything while the other gives in is accommodation or a win-lose result, and compromise needs both sides to give up something.
ww.Both walk away from the table with nothi: Both sides walking away with nothing means no agreement was reached, whereas a compromise yields a settlement that gives each side a partial result.

rw: Each coworker gets half the day, so each gives up part of what they wanted and they meet in the middle, which is a compromise.

ww.Avoidance: Avoidance means dodging the issue without resolving it, but these coworkers talked and agreed on a split, so they directly addressed the conflict and did not avoid it.
ww.A win-lose deal: A win-lose deal gives one person everything and the other nothing, but here each person gets half a day, so the result is shared and not win-lose.
ww.Competition: Competition is trying to win at the other's expense, but these two coworkers agreed to split the day, which is cooperation, so it is not competition.

rw: A vision statement describes the long-term aspiration of an organization, such as becoming the most trusted club in the region by 2030, which gives direction to all later plans.

ww.Club meeting agenda: A club meeting agenda lists the items to discuss at one meeting, so it is a short-term plan, while a statement about being most trusted by 2030 is long term.
ww.Budget line item: A budget line item states an amount of money for a specific expense, and the statement mentions no money, so it is not a budget line item.
ww.Weekly task list: A weekly task list names short-term jobs for a week, while the statement describes a long-term aspiration for 2030, so it does not fit this description.

rw: SMART stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound, five qualities that make a goal clear, trackable, realistic, worthwhile and tied to a deadline.

ww.Speedy, Max, Able, Rich and Top goals se: Speedy, Max, Able, Rich and Top are invented words and not the elements of the SMART goal framework, so this answer is made up.
ww.Simple, Modern, Accurate, Real and Timel: Simple, Modern, Accurate, Real and Timely are not the actual SMART terms, and the real framework has different words, so this list is incorrect.
ww.Strong, Mighty, Active, Ready and Tough: Strong, Mighty, Active, Ready and Tough are only invented adjectives that do not appear in the SMART framework, so this list does not define the acronym.

rw: Raising $2,000 for the food drive by March 31 is specific, measurable with a dollar target, relevant to the drive, and time-bound with a date, so it is the most SMART.

ww.Try to help the community as much as we: Trying to help the community as much as possible has no measurable target or deadline, and it is vague, so it fails the specific, measurable and time-bound parts of SMART.
ww.Do better at fundraising as time goes on: Doing better at fundraising as time goes on gives no amount to measure and no date, so it is vague and cannot be called SMART.
ww.Raise a lot of money soon for the food d: Raising a lot of money soon is vague, because a lot and soon are not measurable amounts or dates, so it lacks the specific and time-bound parts of SMART.

rw: A new competitor entering the market is an external factor that could take away customers and sales, which makes it a threat in a SWOT analysis.

ww.Weakness: A weakness is an internal shortcoming of the organization itself, and a new competitor is an outside factor, so it cannot be classified as a weakness in a SWOT analysis.
ww.Upside: Upside is not one of the four SWOT categories, which are strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats, and a new competitor is not a positive development anyway.
ww.Strength: A strength is an internal advantage that the organization has, but a new competitor is an external factor that harms its position, so it is not a strength.

rw: Contingency planning means preparing responses in advance for unexpected events, such as a supplier failure or a fire, so the organization can react quickly and limit damage.

ww.Planning social events for the staff: Planning social events for staff is event planning for morale and is not about preparing responses to unexpected problems, so it is not contingency planning.
ww.Avoiding all plans for the future of the: Avoiding all plans for the future is the opposite of planning of any kind, so it cannot be contingency planning, which is a careful form of planning.
ww.Planning only for the best case and no r: Planning only for the best case ignores risks, whereas contingency planning deliberately prepares for things going wrong, so it is the opposite of this answer.

rw: The four functions of management are planning, organizing, leading and controlling, which together describe how managers set goals, arrange resources, guide people and check results.

ww.Writing, reading, speaking and listening: Writing, reading, speaking and listening are communication skills and not the four management functions, so this list describes communication and not what managers do.
ww.Saving, spending, lending and borrowing: Saving, spending, lending and borrowing are money activities in personal finance and banking, and they are not the four functions that describe the work of managers.
ww.Buying, selling, hiring and firing worke: Buying, selling, hiring and firing are tasks that managers may do at times, but they are not the four standard management functions of the management process.

rw: Controlling is the function of comparing actual results with goals and taking corrective action when they differ, which is exactly what this manager does.

ww.Organizing: Organizing means arranging people and resources to carry out plans, but comparing results with goals and correcting problems is a different function, so it is not organizing.
ww.Planning: Planning sets goals and decides how to reach them before work begins, but this manager is checking results after the fact, so the function is not planning.
ww.Leading: Leading means motivating and guiding people toward goals, while this manager compares results with goals and corrects problems, which belongs to the controlling function and not leading.

rw: A chain of command is the line of authority running from the top of an organization to the bottom, showing who reports to whom and who gives orders to whom.

ww.A list of company products with their pr: A list of company products with their prices and photos is a catalog, and it says nothing about authority or who reports to whom in the firm.
ww.A set of safety rules posted on the wall: A set of safety rules posted on the walls is a safety policy, and it does not show the lines of authority, so it is not a chain of command.
ww.A group of friends who work in the same: A group of friends in the same office is a social circle and not a formal structure of authority, so it cannot be a chain of command.

rw: A tall organization with many layers passes decisions and messages through many levels, which makes decisions and communication slower and can distort messages along the way.

ww.Equal authority for all of the staff: Equal authority for all staff is a feature of a flat or non-hierarchical firm, but a tall organization has many layers with different levels of authority, so this is wrong.
ww.No managers at all in the firm: A tall organization still has many managers, because the many layers are made of managers, so having no managers at all contradicts the structure.
ww.Faster decisions with fewer steps: Faster decisions with fewer steps describe a flat organization, while a tall one passes decisions through many layers, which makes the process slower, so this option is reversed.

rw: A flat organizational structure has few management levels and wide spans of control, which gives faster communication and decisions and gives employees more independence.

ww.A structure with many levels of managers: A structure with many levels of managers is a tall structure, and a flat structure has the opposite, so this describes the wrong type.
ww.A structure with no employees at all: A structure with no employees cannot run a business, so it is not a real description of a flat structure, which still has many employees.
ww.A structure with only one product line: A structure with only one product line is about what a firm sells, whereas flat and tall describe levels of management, so this has nothing to do with the term.

rw: A performance appraisal is a review of an employee's work against expectations and goals, which gives feedback, guides pay and promotion decisions and helps plan improvement and development.

ww.A plan for a company party that managers: A plan for a company party is an event plan and has nothing to do with judging how well an employee does their job, so it is not an appraisal.
ww.A tax on wages paid to workers and staff: A tax on wages paid to workers is a payroll deduction collected by government, and it does not evaluate how well an employee performs, so it is not an appraisal.
ww.A list of job openings in the company's: A list of job openings is a recruiting notice for filling positions, and it does not review the work of current employees, so it is not a performance appraisal.

rw: Self-actualization, which means reaching one's full potential, sits at the top of Maslow's hierarchy, and people usually pursue it only after their lower needs are mostly met.

ww.Safety and security: Safety and security needs sit on the second level of Maslow's hierarchy, just above basic physical needs, so they are near the bottom and not the highest need.
ww.Physiological needs: Physiological needs, such as food, water and sleep, form the base of the hierarchy, so they are the lowest level and not the highest need.
ww.Social belonging: Social belonging is the third level of Maslow's hierarchy, in the middle, so it ranks above safety needs but below esteem and self-actualization, and is not the highest.

rw: Paying rent affects shelter and financial security, which are physiological and safety needs at the base of Maslow's hierarchy, so this worker is focused on that level.

ww.Belonging and social needs: Belonging and social needs rank above safety, and a worker worried about paying rent is concerned about survival and stability and not about friendship or belonging.
ww.Self-actualization at the top: Self-actualization is the top level, which people pursue after basic needs are met, so a worker anxious about rent is not mainly focused on it.
ww.Esteem and respect from others: Esteem and respect from others is a higher level, and a worker worried about rent is still concerned with basic needs, so esteem is not the main focus now.

rw: Herzberg's motivators are factors such as achievement, recognition and growth, which come from the work itself and create real satisfaction and motivation, unlike hygiene factors.

ww.Strict rules and close supervision: Strict rules and close supervision are company policy and supervision factors, which Herzberg called hygiene factors; they prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate, so they are not motivators.
ww.Salary and working conditions only: Salary and working conditions are hygiene factors in Herzberg's theory, which prevent dissatisfaction but do not by themselves motivate, so they are not motivators.
ww.Office temperature and lighting levels: Office temperature and lighting levels are working conditions, which Herzberg classed as hygiene factors, so they prevent dissatisfaction without motivating employees and are not motivators.

rw: Intrinsic motivation comes from within, such as enjoyment or a sense of purpose, and a student who joins because they love helping others is driven by that inner satisfaction.

ww.Coercion by a boss: Coercion by a boss means being forced or threatened, but the student joins willingly because they love helping others, so no one is forcing them.
ww.Compliance with rules: Compliance with rules means acting because one must, but the student joins by choice and for enjoyment, so it is not compliance.
ww.Extrinsic motivation: Extrinsic motivation comes from outside rewards or pressures such as pay or praise, but this student is driven by a love of helping, which is internal.

rw: A code of ethics is a set of principles that guide acceptable behavior in an organization, helping employees make honest, fair decisions and showing customers what standards the firm follows.

ww.A tax form filed each year by companies: A tax form filed each year to report profits is a financial document for authorities, and it does not describe principles for acceptable behavior in an organization.
ww.A list of product prices set by the sale: A list of product prices set by the sales department is a price list, and it does not set out rules of conduct, so it is not a code of ethics.
ww.A schedule of meetings held by managers: A schedule of meetings held by managers is a calendar of events and does not state principles of behavior, so it cannot be a code of ethics.

rw: Reporting falsified reports through the proper channel, such as a supervisor or ethics hotline, handles the problem fairly and protects the organization, so it is the best first step.

ww.Ignore it to avoid trouble at work: Ignoring the falsification to avoid trouble allows dishonesty to continue and may cause harm to the organization, so staying silent is not an ethical response.
ww.Gossip about it with other coworkers: Gossiping with coworkers spreads rumors, does not fix the problem and may hurt a person unfairly, so it is not a proper way to deal with misconduct.
ww.Copy the false reports for yourself: Copying the false reports for yourself does not address the dishonesty and could create trouble for you, so it is not a proper first step.

rw: A conflict of interest is a situation where personal interests, such as a relationship or financial stake, could influence or appear to influence a person's professional duties and judgment.

ww.A routine meeting held every week by the: A routine weekly meeting to review work is normal business activity and involves no clash between personal and professional duties, so it is not a conflict of interest.
ww.A disagreement over lunch plans between: A disagreement over lunch plans is a personal difference of opinion with no effect on professional duties, so it is not a conflict of interest, which concerns divided loyalties.
ww.A friendly competition between two teams: A friendly competition between teams for a prize is ordinary rivalry and does not pit personal interests against professional duties, so it is not a conflict of interest.

rw: The four main functions of management are planning, organizing, leading and controlling, which together cover setting goals, arranging resources, directing people and checking results.

ww.Buying, selling, storing and shipping go: Buying, selling, storing and shipping goods are trade and logistics activities, and they are not the four functions of management, which are planning, organizing, leading and controlling.
ww.Saving, spending, lending and borrowing: Saving, spending, lending and borrowing are personal finance or banking actions, and they do not describe the four functions through which managers run an organization.
ww.Hiring, firing, paying and training staf: Hiring, firing, paying and training staff are human resource tasks, which fall under some functions, but they are not the four main functions of management.

rw: Planning involves setting goals and deciding how to achieve them, including choosing actions and resources, so it gives direction to the other management functions that follow.

ww.Measuring results only after the work is: Measuring results after the work is done describes controlling, which compares outcomes with goals, so it is a different function from planning that takes place before work begins.
ww.Motivating staff and guiding them each d: Motivating staff and guiding them each day is the leading function, which deals with directing people, so it is not the planning function.
ww.Arranging resources only, such as people: Arranging resources such as people and tools is the organizing function, which follows planning, so it does not describe planning, which sets goals and chooses how to reach them.

rw: Top-level management consists of executives, such as the CEO and president, who set the overall strategy and direction for the entire organization and are accountable for its results.

ww.Entry-level employees who do routine dai: Entry-level employees who do routine daily tasks are operational workers and not managers, so they are not top-level management, which sets direction for the whole organization.
ww.Department assistants who support the st: Department assistants who support the staff are support employees without strategic authority, so they are not top-level management, which holds the highest decision-making roles.
ww.Supervisors of daily work who give order: Supervisors of daily work who give orders to staff are first-line managers at the lowest management level, so they are not top-level management.

rw: Middle managers carry out the plans of top management and oversee first-line supervisors, so they link the strategy set at the top to the daily work done below.

ww.Frontline workers who do the tasks that: Frontline workers who do the tasks the firm sells are operational employees and not managers, so they are not middle management, which supervises other managers.
ww.Interns who work for a short period to l: Interns who work briefly to learn the job are trainees without management authority, so they are not middle managers, who hold a real responsibility for departments.
ww.Executives who set the long-term strateg: Executives who set the long-term strategy are top management, which sits above middle management, so this describes the wrong level of the organization.

rw: First-line managers are supervisors who oversee the daily work of non-managerial employees, which makes them the lowest management level and the link between workers and middle managers.

ww.Board directors who are elected by the s: Board directors elected by shareholders govern the company at the highest level, so they are above management, and they are not first-line managers who supervise daily work.
ww.Executives who set the strategy for the: Executives who set the strategy for the whole company are top managers, who sit at the highest level, so they are not first-line managers.
ww.Investors who own shares of the company: Investors who own shares of the company are owners, not managers, and voting at meetings is an ownership right, so they are not first-line management.

rw: Conceptual skills are the ability to see the organization as a whole and think strategically, which top managers need most because they set direction and handle complex problems.

ww.Fast typing speed: Fast typing speed is a basic clerical skill, and top managers do not need it most, since their work centers on strategy and big-picture judgment.
ww.Cleaning-up skills: Cleaning-up skills relate to janitorial work and are not a management skill, so they are not what top managers need most to lead an organization.
ww.Technical skills only: Technical skills only would be too narrow for top managers, who rely more on conceptual skills, since their work involves strategy and not hands-on technical tasks.

rw: Human or interpersonal skills are the ability to communicate, motivate and work well with people, which every level of manager needs to lead teams and build good relationships.

ww.Mechanical repair skills: Mechanical repair skills are technical abilities for fixing machines and have no link to working well with people, so they are not the interpersonal management skill asked about.
ww.Technical job skills only: Technical job skills only cover task knowledge and not dealing with people, so they do not describe the skill of working well with others.
ww.Conceptual skills for the whole: Conceptual skills involve seeing the whole organization and thinking strategically, and they concern ideas more than people, so they do not describe working well with others.

rw: Technical skills are the specific knowledge and proficiency needed to perform a particular job, such as accounting or machine operation, and first-line managers rely on them most.

ww.People skills, including how to work wel: People skills for working with colleagues are human or interpersonal skills, which are a separate category of management skills, so they are not technical skills.
ww.Big-picture thinking about the strategy: Big-picture thinking about the whole firm is a conceptual skill, which is another category of management skill, so it is not what technical skills mean.
ww.Public speaking only in front of large a: Public speaking only in front of large crowds is a narrow communication ability, and technical skills mean job-specific knowledge, so this option does not define them.

rw: Mintzberg's interpersonal roles are figurehead, leader and liaison, which describe a manager's ceremonial duties, guidance of employees and links with people outside the unit.

ww.Analyst, auditor and clerk: Analyst, auditor and clerk are not Mintzberg's interpersonal roles, so this list of job titles does not match the figurehead, leader and liaison roles he described.
ww.Buyer, seller and banker only: Buyer, seller and banker are business occupations and not Mintzberg's interpersonal roles, so this list is not part of his model of what managers do.
ww.Driver, cook and cleaner only: Driver, cook and cleaner are ordinary jobs and not Mintzberg's managerial roles, so this list is unrelated to the interpersonal roles of a manager.

rw: Delegation means assigning a task to a capable person and giving them the authority to decide how to complete it, which is exactly what this manager does with the project.

ww.Micromanaging: Micromanaging means controlling every detail of someone's work, but this manager gives the employee authority to decide, so the behavior is the opposite of micromanaging.
ww.Abdication: Abdication means abandoning responsibility entirely, but this manager hands over the project to a capable person with authority and still remains accountable, so it is not abdication.
ww.Termination: Termination means ending someone's employment, but this manager is giving the employee more responsibility, not ending her job, so it does not describe the situation.

rw: A narrow span of control means a manager supervises few employees, which allows closer supervision and more individual attention, though it can lead to a taller structure with more layers.

ww.Supervises many employees loosely: Supervising many employees loosely is a wide span of control, which is the opposite of a narrow span, so this describes the wrong type.
ww.Supervises no one at all in the firm: Supervising no one at all would mean the person is not a manager, so it cannot describe a manager with a narrow span, who still supervises a few people.
ww.Works only with the executives: Working only with executives is not what span of control describes, since it measures how many subordinates report to a manager, and a narrow span means few, not executives.

rw: A tall organizational structure has many levels of management and narrow spans of control, so each manager supervises few people, which slows communication but gives close supervision.

ww.A structure with no managers, where all: A structure with no managers and equal decisions is a flat or leaderless arrangement, not a tall structure, which has many levels of management.
ww.A structure with few levels of managemen: A structure with few levels and wide spans of control is a flat structure, which is the opposite of a tall organizational structure, so this answer is reversed.
ww.A structure for small shops with a singl: A structure for small shops with a single owner is a simple structure, and a tall structure is about many levels of management, so it does not describe a tall one.

rw: In a matrix structure, employees report to both a functional manager and a project manager, which combines specialized expertise with project focus, though it can cause conflicting demands.

ww.A structure with no bosses, in which all: A structure with no bosses, in which everyone shares equal authority, is a flat or self-managed arrangement, and a matrix structure has managers and reporting lines, so this is wrong.
ww.A structure with one boss at the top who: One boss at the top who makes all decisions describes a centralized or autocratic structure, whereas a matrix has employees reporting to more than one manager, so this is incorrect.
ww.A structure of a single product made and: A single product made and sold by one department is a simple functional setup, while a matrix combines functions with projects, so this does not describe a matrix structure.

rw: A divisional structure groups activities by product, market or geography, with each division running semi-independently, which lets each unit respond to its own customers and conditions.

ww.Having one manager only, who controls al: Having one manager who controls all activities describes a simple centralized structure, whereas a divisional structure splits the firm into semi-independent divisions, so this is incorrect.
ww.Grouping by function, so each department: Grouping by function, so each department handles one kind of work like sales or finance, is a functional structure, which differs from the divisional approach of grouping by product or market.
ww.Having no groups at all, so that every e: Having no groups at all, so every employee works alone, is not an organizational structure that firms use, and it does not describe a divisional structure with distinct divisions.

rw: Centralization means concentrating decision-making authority at the top of the organization, so senior managers make most key choices, which gives consistency and control but can slow responses.

ww.Spreading authority widely to many lower: Spreading authority widely to many lower levels is decentralization, which is the opposite of centralization, where decision-making power is kept at the top of the organization.
ww.Moving offices to a new building or city: Moving offices to a new building or city is a relocation decision about where a firm is based, and it does not describe who holds decision-making authority.
ww.Closing branches that do not make a prof: Closing unprofitable branches is a restructuring decision about operations, and it has nothing to do with whether authority is concentrated at the top, so it is not centralization.

rw: Decentralization means pushing decision-making authority down to lower levels, which speeds decisions, uses local knowledge and motivates employees, though it can reduce consistency across the organization.

ww.Keeping all decisions at the top with se: Keeping all decisions at the top with senior managers is centralization, which is the opposite of decentralization, so this answer describes the wrong concept.
ww.Cutting staff to save money in the firm: Cutting staff to save money is downsizing, a cost-saving measure, and it does not describe where decision-making authority sits, so it is not decentralization.
ww.Closing the company and selling off all: Closing the company and selling off its assets is liquidation, the ending of a business, and it has no connection to spreading decision-making authority to lower levels.

rw: An organization chart is a diagram that shows the structure of roles and reporting relationships, making clear who reports to whom and how the parts of the organization connect.

ww.A shift schedule that shows which worker: A shift schedule showing who is on duty is a staffing roster, and it does not show the structure of roles and reporting lines, so it is not an organization chart.
ww.A sales graph that shows how much a comp: A sales graph showing how much a company sells over time is a performance chart, and it does not show roles or who reports to whom, so it is not this chart.
ww.A financial statement showing assets, de: A financial statement showing assets, debts and profits is an accounting report about money, and it does not display roles or reporting lines, so it is not an organization chart.

rw: Unity of command means each employee reports to only one supervisor, which avoids conflicting orders and makes accountability clear, since everyone knows exactly whom to answer to.

ww.Employees choose their own bosses freely: Employees choosing their own bosses freely would cause confusion, and unity of command is about a single fixed supervisor for each person, so this answer does not match.
ww.No supervisors exist anywhere in the fir: No supervisors existing anywhere would remove all reporting lines, but unity of command depends on supervisors, with each employee having exactly one, so this option contradicts it.
ww.Everyone reports to everyone, with many: Everyone reporting to everyone with many bosses is the opposite of unity of command, because it creates conflicting orders and unclear responsibility rather than a single clear reporting line.

rw: Accountability in management means being answerable for results and decisions, so a manager must explain outcomes and accept responsibility for both successes and failures, which builds trust in the organization.

ww.Delegating blame to others for mistakes: Delegating blame to others for mistakes dodges responsibility, whereas accountability means accepting answerability yourself, so shifting blame is the opposite of being accountable.
ww.Avoiding blame for any mistakes made at: Avoiding blame for any mistakes at work is the opposite of accountability, which requires taking responsibility for outcomes, so dodging blame fails the definition of the term.
ww.Having no duties or tasks to carry out a: Having no duties or tasks to carry out leaves nothing to be accountable for, and accountability depends on responsibilities that a person must answer for, so this is wrong.
